newsitem.title: CHINA: China plans to restructure inefficient car industry.
newsitem.headline: China plans to restructure inefficient car industry.

text.p: China is planning a major restructuring of its car and truck industry to increase efficiency, analysts said on Friday.

Geng Shaojie, general manager of China's largest vehicle manufacturer, First Automotive Group, was quoted in the Shanghai-based Business News as calling for swift official action to rationalise the industry.
He proposed the closure of smaller, inefficient auto producers and urged the government not to approve any more manufacturing plants before 2000.
China's auto market is in the doldrums because of overproduction, a steady flow of imports and stockpiles of 250,000 vehicles with sales continuing to lag well behind supply, analysts say.

Demand in 1997 is estimated at 1.66 million units with production at 1.65 million but imports of around 120,000 vehicles per year and stockpiles would bring the supply level up to well over two million, the Shanghai Securites News said early this month.
Officials have said they want to create three or four major auto groups, but the process is being blocked by local authorities who want to protect their own plants, analysts say.

"The development of China's automobile industry has lost its balance," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage. "China has too many small-scale car manufacturers, whose quality and quantity cannot meet demand."
China currently had 160 vehicle manufacturers, but most could only produce a few thousand vehicles a year, while some could only produce a few hundred, the Shanghai Securities News said.
About 30 smaller firms would soon be forced to merge with larger manufacturers or apply for bankruptcy, the paper said.

"If China wants to improve the efficiency of its automobile industry, some major restructuring is necessary," a Shanghai industrial analyst said. "The problem of investment duplication particularly is holding back further development."
More than two-thirds of China's 30 provinces and municipalities had marked the auto industry as a key sector for growth and were continuing to pour in investment capital, analysts said.

"Many of these provinces focusing on developing automobile production have imposed protectionist policies to prevent inroads by competitors from other provinces," said an official with a major auto plant in northern China. "This is not beneficial for creating a healthy market and has resulted in problems in boosting the scale of production and increasing the efficiency of producers overall," he said.
First Automotive, based in the northeast city of Changchun, produced 250,000 vehicles in 1996, including 200 kinds of trucks and cars.
Shanghai Volkswagen Co, a joint venture between Germany's Volkswagen AG and Shanghai Automotive Industry (Group) Corp (SAIC), sold 196,000.
SAIC is also involved in a $1 billion joint venture with General Motors Corp to build a plant in Shanghai's Pudong New Area with a projected annual capacity of 100,000 mid-sized luxury sedan cars.
The GM plant, which is awaiting final official approval, is scheduled to go into production by the end of 1998.

"Competition will become more fierce with more foreign auto makers entering the domestic market," said a Shanghai-based industrial analyst. "It looks like the small vehicle makers are going to face some hard times."

As a result of the stagnant market, the southern province of Guangdong and the central city of Chongqing recently decided not to designate the auto sector as a "pillar" industry in their economies, local media reported early this month.
